analysis.one_liner: Exempts farm animal waste, manure, and fertilizer from federal waste-cleanup law and limits citizen lawsuits against farms.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 68 cosponsors, including 11 Democrats, but never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the nation's solid waste law, the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, to say that animal waste, manure, and fertilizer coming from or used by a farm are not covered — even when runoff from them contaminates water or soil. It would also bar citizens from filing suits under that law against a farm whenever a federal or state agency is already pursuing enforcement, or when a state's own approved plan covers the practice. The bill never advanced past its initial referral to a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural operations — especially large livestock, dairy, and poultry operations that generate huge volumes of manure — would gain exemption from federal waste requirements and protection from private citizen suits over manure-related contamination, as long as a government enforcement action is nominally underway.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds animal waste, manure, fertilizer, and constituents derived from them to the statutory definition of excluded material whenever they originate from or are used by an agricultural operation, removing them from the Solid Waste Disposal Act's requirements.

It would block citizen suits against an agricultural operation when the EPA or a state is 'diligently seeking compliance' in an administrative proceeding, is prosecuting a civil or criminal action, has opened an administrative proceeding, or when the alleged violation falls under a state-approved plan.

The bill states a purpose of providing 'legal clarity' to entities attempting to comply with state or federal environmental permits and standards, framing the change as shielding farms from what its findings call judicial misinterpretation of the waste law.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near large farms — particularly those whose wells and waterways can be contaminated by manure and fertilizer runoff — would lose a legal tool to force cleanup when government enforcement is absent or slow. Taxpayers could also bear cleanup costs that private suits would otherwise shift to polluters.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rural residents near large livestock operations

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip residents of the ability to sue a farm under the waste law whenever any federal or state enforcement proceeding is pending, even one a community considers inadequate, leaving neighbors dependent entirely on agency discretion.

Manure and fertilizer runoff is a leading source of nitrate contamination in rural groundwater, and a blanket statutory exclusion of these materials and their 'constituents' would remove them from the federal waste-cleanup framework rather than relying on performance standards.

The bar on citizen suits triggered by a state-approved plan means the level of protection would vary by state, since the suit is blocked whether or not the state plan is actually enforced against the specific operation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real value to farm operators: predictability, and freedom from private lawsuits and federal waste-law liability over manure handling. But the cost falls on a different group of people — the rural residents downstream and down-gradient of those operations, who would lose one of the few enforcement tools that works when agencies do not act. The bill addresses a genuine legal ambiguity for farmers, but it does so by removing recourse from the people affected by the pollution rather than by setting enforceable standards for it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment Subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Newhouse introduced the bill on February 3, 2017, with about 30 original cosponsors from both parties, largely members from agricultural districts.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on February 3, 2017, and to the Subcommittee on Environment on February 10, 2017.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee vote, was never debated on the House floor, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill ultimately accumulated 68 cosponsors — 57 Republicans and 11 Democrats — but that support never translated into any committee or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rural communities near large livestock operations keep their existing right to sue under the federal waste law, and large farm operators did not receive the exemption from it. The status quo — where manure can be challenged in court under RCRA — continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rural residents who can still sue under federal waste law

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship skewed heavily Republican — 57 Republicans to 11 Democrats — with Democratic support coming mainly from rural and agricultural districts.

industries.note: The bill would exempt their manure and waste from the federal solid waste law and shield them from citizen suits whenever any government proceeding is pending. Their gain comes directly at the expense of neighbors' ability to force cleanup of manure-contaminated water and soil.

The exemption covers fertilizer originating from or used by any agricultural operation, giving smaller and diversified farms the same regulatory certainty as large ones. The public-health cost of weakening water-pollution recourse falls on communities near all of these operations, though the largest manure producers benefit most.

Citizen suits under the waste law are a core tool these groups and affected residents use to address contamination when agencies do not act; the bill narrows that tool specifically for agricultural operations.
